title: Reflecting on my research interests
body:
My research trajectory has never remained stagnant. It's a "cool" way to start, I know. Some might even call it a mercurial pursuit and think it shows a lack of long-term commitment. But I genuinely feel that this fluidity can be a strength, as long as I am actually building knowledge and the right skills along the way. My words probably make it obvious that I am an early-stage researcher from Gen Z.

I am constantly moved and motivated by the sheer number of interesting developments happening in science. I understand the traditional view that a tree with deep, established roots is harder to remove than one with shallow roots, and I do agree that depth matters. But we also know that different trees flourish in different environments, and sometimes luck matters too. I didn't believe in luck for a long time, but I have realised how crazy luck can work. I hope we all get lucky, because why not?

For me, being interested in many areas does not automatically mean being a master of none. I think it means I am still figuring out where my strongest questions are and where I want to build real depth. I am not trying to justify changing interests. I am simply embracing the process of discovering what genuinely stays with me.

My research journey may look chaotic right now, but I honestly feel like I am in the right and the wrong era at the same time. There is so much happening, and that makes choosing one narrow path difficult, but also exciting.

That is really the main reason I created this page. I wanted one place to collect my research interests, my perspective, and the literature I have explored, am exploring, and will probably keep exploring.
excerpt: My research trajectory has never really stayed in one place, and I am learning to see that curiosity as a strength rather than something I need to hide.

title: Semiconductor industry
body:
The semiconductor industry has been growing rapidly ever since it was introduced because semiconductors are part of almost everything we use or come across today, from smartphones and electric vehicles to artificial intelligence and quantum computing. What interested me was not only how much the industry has grown, but how many times it has reinvented itself.

The actual semiconductor revolution began with the transition from vacuum tubes to transistors, followed by integrated circuits and then microprocessors. That enabled computing, communication and automation at a completely different scale.

The industry is broadly discussed through analog and digital chips. Analog chips process real-world signals, while digital chips work with binary information and include processors, memory and logic devices.

Semiconductor fabrication itself involves hundreds of processes. Broadly, it can be divided into front-end wafer fabrication and back-end testing and packaging. The major steps include wafer manufacturing, oxidation, photolithography, etching, deposition, ion implantation, metal wiring, testing and finally packaging.

By the 2010s, semiconductor production had also become geographically specialised. Design, fabrication, assembly and packaging were often happening in different parts of the world. The fabless and foundry model became especially important, where fabless companies focused mainly on design and foundries manufactured those designs.

At the same time, smartphones, tablets, IoT, cloud computing and data centres increased the need for faster and more energy-efficient chips. Chip design itself became more complex and moved towards multicore and heterogeneous architectures, which also increased the importance of simulation tools, design software and skilled people.

The 2020s brought another major shift because of artificial intelligence. The demand for data centres, GPUs, accelerators, advanced memory and edge computing devices increased rapidly. At the same time, supply-chain disruptions and geopolitical tensions made countries think more seriously about semiconductor self-reliance.

What I find most interesting is that the semiconductor industry is no longer only about making smaller transistors. Materials, architecture, system integration, packaging, energy efficiency, cost, manufacturing, supply chains and even geopolitics are all connected now.

Over the last few decades, semiconductors have gone from being mainly a manufacturing technology to becoming a major part of global innovation and strategy. Looking ahead, I think the field will keep changing based on how well it balances innovation, performance, cost and the increasingly complex global ecosystem around it.
excerpt: I wanted to understand why semiconductors keep appearing in almost every conversation about present and future technology.

title: My Journey into Science
body:
I have always been fascinated by science since I was a child. The journey has been chaotic and, to be honest, I wasn't always as serious as I should have been. Yet throughout it all, it has been me fighting against myself more than anything else. I was curious, emotional, ambitious, confused and hopeful, often all at once.

If I look back, I think the person who has influenced me the most is Kalpana Chawla. She entered my life at a time when I realised that science was not just a single subject but an entire universe waiting to be explored. There have been many other role models along the way, but she has left the deepest impression on me.

My scientific journey has been anything but linear. It began with my love for organic chemistry, shifted towards physics, wandered into biological sciences and eventually brought me back to chemistry. For the longest time, I kept searching for my "master subject", believing there had to be one field that defined me. But with interdisciplinary research becoming more common, and now AI changing the way we approach science, I have started to realise that perhaps there was never meant to be just one path.

I chose pure sciences after many inspiring conversations with one of my seniors, who shared stories about his research. Listening to those stories made me realise that I wanted to become a researcher myself, and somewhere during those conversations, the dream of pursuing a PhD quietly took shape.

During my bachelor's, I had the opportunity to work on a small research project involving a survey on women with PCOS. Collecting reliable data was far from easy. Social stigma meant that many women were understandably hesitant to disclose accurate information, so we had to work carefully with the responses we received. Despite these challenges, it was an incredibly informative experience. I took the work seriously and eventually submitted a report with conclusions drawn from the survey data. It was my first glimpse into the realities of research, where perfect data is rare and thoughtful interpretation matters just as much.

During my master's, I spent a month at a CSIR laboratory for an internship. That month became one of the most memorable phases of my academic life. I attended a scientific conference, got exposure to NMR instrumentation and worked on enhancing the curcumin content in oleoresin. I documented the entire work in the form of a detailed report.

More importantly, it was my first real laboratory experience. My guide, the PhD scholars and the project associates welcomed me warmly, patiently answered my endless questions and made the entire experience unforgettable. They taught me not only scientific techniques but also what a research environment actually feels like.

After the internship, my work shifted into an interdisciplinary space involving inorganic chemistry, polymers and applied physics, while allowing me to build on the analytical chemistry skills I had already developed. Synthesising the material, confirming its formation, improving its thermal stability, encapsulating the perovskite and finally fabricating it into a triboelectric nanogenerator for UV sensing was challenging at every step.

Seeing that work eventually lead to a publication in a Q1 journal felt surreal. Equally memorable was presenting the work at different conferences and symposiums. Every presentation brought a different audience, different questions and different perspectives. It was stressful, definitely, but also incredibly rewarding. Those experiences taught me how to communicate science, defend my work, interact with researchers and appreciate how collaborative research really is.

My growing interest in semiconductors eventually led me to apply for a project position at IIT Palakkad. After clearing the interview, I moved there to work on semiconductor-related research. It became another defining chapter of my journey. For the first time, I was largely on my own as a researcher, with guidance from my supervisor and support from wonderful colleagues. Even though I had moved to an unfamiliar place, it quickly began to feel like home.

Being at IIT Palakkad also gave me opportunities I had never imagined. I attended inspiring talks by Prof. H. C. Verma, Arunachalam Muruganantham, and several distinguished scientists from national laboratories and research institutions across India and abroad. Listening to them, interacting with researchers from different backgrounds and seeing their passion for what they do broadened my perspective far beyond the laboratory.

When I look back today, I don't see a perfectly planned journey. I see detours, uncertainty, failed experiments, changing interests and countless moments of self-doubt. But I also see growth. Every subject I explored, every laboratory I entered, every experiment that failed, every conference presentation that made me nervous and every conversation with mentors and fellow researchers shaped the scientist I am still becoming.

I don't know exactly where this journey will lead next, and perhaps that's the most exciting part. Science has never been about reaching a final destination. It is about continuing to ask questions, embracing uncertainty and finding joy in discovering something new.

This is only the beginning.
excerpt: My scientific journey has never been linear. It has been curiosity, confusion, research, good mentors, failed experiments and a lot of learning.

title: Polymer Surfaces, Adhesion and Interfaces
excerpt: This was one of the talks I connected with the most because it was close to the kind of materials questions I already enjoy thinking about.
body:
This was probably one of the talks I connected with the most because it was very close to the kind of materials and interface questions I already enjoy thinking about.

A major part of the talk was about polymer surfaces and why adhesion can be difficult. Polymers generally have low surface energy, so sometimes the surface has to be modified before another material can stick to it properly.

Plasma treatment was one of the methods discussed, and silanes were also mentioned as adhesion promoters.

One distinction I found really useful was the difference between an interface and an interphase. An interface is basically the boundary between two materials, while an interphase has a certain thickness because of the interactions happening between the coating and the substrate.

Another point that stayed with me was the locus of failure. If adhesion fails, just saying that the material failed is not enough. We need to know where it failed.

The talk also covered XPS, contact angle measurements and superhydrophobic surfaces. I had always associated superhydrophobicity mainly with a very high contact angle, but the talk also discussed tilt angle and contact angle hysteresis.

There was also discussion about acid base interactions, laser treatment and different dry and wet methods for modifying polymer surfaces.

What I liked most was that the talk made something that sounds simple, making two materials stick together, feel much more interesting. Surface chemistry, roughness, treatment, energy, the interface or interphase and the actual failure mechanism all start mattering at the same time.

title: Solid-State Batteries: From Materials to the Cell
excerpt: I liked how this talk connected ion transport and materials all the way to actual cell-level problems.
body:
I liked this talk because it moved from what is happening at the atomic level all the way to what happens inside an actual cell and eventually a module.

Different battery systems were discussed, including lithium ion, lithium metal and solid state batteries. One of the basic differences that stood out to me was replacing a liquid electrolyte with a solid electrolyte.

But of course, changing one component does not magically solve everything.

A major challenge discussed was dendrite growth. Lithium dendrites can penetrate the solid electrolyte and eventually lead to failure, which makes the stability of both the electrolyte and the electrode electrolyte interface really important.

The talk also covered different ways ions can move through solids, including direct hopping, interstitial hopping and vacancy mediated hopping.

I liked this part because it made the connection between material structure and device performance feel very direct. Something happening at an atomic scale eventually becomes a problem we can see at the cell level.

Modelling was also discussed, including properties such as ionic conductivity, stability and thermodynamic behaviour. COMSOL was mentioned as one of the tools used for simulation.

For sulphide based solid electrolytes, careful handling is important because the materials can be sensitive to the environment, which is why glove box preparation becomes relevant.

My main takeaway was that battery performance cannot really be reduced to just finding a good cathode or anode. Ion transport, interfaces, stability, materials processing and cell design are all connected.

title: Research, Startups and Industry
excerpt: This talk made me think about what research can become beyond papers and the academic lab.
body:
This talk was less about one particular material and more about what can happen to research after it leaves the academic lab.

One part I found interesting was the journey from a patent to a startup. Research does not always have to end with a paper. Sometimes the work can move towards a product, a company or an actual industry problem.

That idea stayed with me because I have always liked the thought of building something that is actually mine someday.

The speaker also talked about technical skills and interdisciplinary knowledge. I agree with that because research careers are not always as structured as they look from the outside. Sometimes knowing how to connect different skills becomes just as useful as knowing one thing very deeply.

AI also came up as a tool for saving time and improving productivity. Prompting was discussed too, because the way we ask a question can completely change the kind of output we get.

Another point was doing internships during a PhD and the possibility of working on industry linked PhD projects. I liked that because it gives another way of seeing what research looks like outside the university environment.

What I took from this talk was that research can move in many directions. Papers are one part of it, but patents, startups, industry collaborations and technology development can also become part of the same journey.

title: Aerospace: Materials, Technology and Careers
excerpt: This was outside my immediate area, but the overlap with materials, AI and industry still made it interesting to me.
body:
This talk was quite far from my immediate research area, but I still found parts of it interesting because materials, data and technology somehow kept appearing everywhere.

The speaker discussed sustainable aviation fuel, supersonic aircraft, high temperature materials, smart materials, smart structures and some of the newer technologies being explored in aerospace.

AI and machine learning were also discussed in the context of aircraft data. Aircraft generate a huge amount of information during operation, and that data can be used for monitoring, analysis and digital twin development.

There was also discussion about metallic and composite aircraft, CAD/CAM, GD&T and virtual prototypes.

The career part was interesting too. One point was that getting into a large company does not always happen by simply submitting an application and waiting. Networking and employee referrals can matter.

The speaker also stressed the importance of fundamentals, which I completely agreed with. I keep getting reminded of this in different areas. Breadth is useful, but without fundamentals it becomes very easy to only know things at the surface level.

Another point that stayed with me was scientific communication. Most scientific papers are written for scientists, but there is also value in being able to explain science to people who are not from that field.

Aerospace is not the area I am currently working in, but I liked seeing how materials, computation, engineering and industry come together in a completely different space.
